title: South Korea's Short-Drama App Users Top 5 Million — All Top 5 Are Chinese-Owned
text:
South Korea's Short-Drama App Users Top 5 Million — All Top 5 Are Chinese-Owned — BigGo Finance Ask AI Real-time News Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast Market Influencers Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast Market Influencers More Ask AI Real-time News Watchlist Holdings Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Podcast Market Influencers South Korea's Short-Drama App Users Top 5 Million — All Top 5 Are Chinese-Owned
 Add preferred source Combined monthly active users across South Korea's 10 major short-drama apps reached about 5.07 million last month, nearly tripling in a year. All five of the most-used apps are Chinese-owned, led by DramaBox at 1.19 million, followed by NetShort, FreeReels and DramaWave. In new installs, NetShort topped the entertainment category with 750,000 downloads, and the five Chinese-owned apps together drew nearly 2.16 million new installs in October. AI-driven production that sharply cuts cost and production time is cited as their competitive edge, while calls are growing for regulatory fixes to close gaps in youth protection. Key Elements 
 DramaBox NetShort FreeReels DramaWave ReelShort Vigloo Spoon Labs Krafton Lezhin Snack Wiseapp·Retail Mobile Index YouTube Short-form dramas — the vertical-video genre that hooks viewers with a plot twist every one to two minutes — are spreading fast in South Korea, pushing monthly users of short-drama apps past 5 million. The audience has nearly tripled in a year, and Chinese-owned platforms mass-producing content with artificial intelligence are effectively monopolizing the top of the popularity rankings.
 According to data released on Nov. 18 by market research firm Wiseapp·Retail, the 10 major short-drama apps in South Korea had a combined 5.07 million monthly active users (MAU) last month, up 197.4% from 1.7 million in October last year.
 All five of the most-used apps are Chinese-owned. China's DramaBox led with 1.19 million users, followed by NetShort (1.12 million), FreeReels (760,000) and DramaWave (680,000). ReelShort, operated by U.S.-based Crazy Maple Studio, ranked fifth with 500,000 users, but is effectively classified as Chinese-owned because Chinese publisher COL Group is its largest shareholder with a 49.24% stake.
 Rank App Monthly Active Users (MAU) Note 
 1 DramaBox 1.19 million Chinese-owned 
 2 NetShort 1.12 million Chinese-owned 
 3 FreeReels 760,000 Chinese-owned 
 4 DramaWave 680,000 Chinese-owned 
 5 ReelShort 500,000 COL Group holds 49.24% stake 
 6 Vigloo 400,000 Operated by Spoon Labs 
 7 Lezhin Snack 170,000 Affiliate of Lezhin Entertainment 
 Note: Based on the 10 major short-drama apps in South Korea tracked by Wiseapp·Retail; monthly active users last month.
 Vigloo, the South Korean platform run by Krafton-backed Spoon Labs, ranked sixth with 400,000 users, and Lezhin Snack, a unit of Lezhin Entertainment, was seventh with 170,000. Chinese-owned apps thus captured about 80% of all users.
 Short dramas are ultra-short video series, each episode running just one to two minutes, structured as serialized installments that pull viewers into the next episode. They are typically produced in runs of 50 to 100 episodes and lean on provocative material — romance, affairs, chaebol families, revenge and secret birth origins — that triggers a quick reward response. According to Vigloo, the core South Korean audience is women aged 35 and older, who make up more than half of viewers.
 Chinese-owned apps also stand out in new installs. According to app analytics platform Mobile Index, NetShort logged 750,000 new installs last month, ranking first in the entertainment category and far outpacing downloads of TVING (470,000), Coupang Play (310,000) and Netflix (290,000) over the same period.
 South Korean mobile users on iOS and Android downloaded FreeReels 420,000 times during the period, DramaBox 390,000 times, ReelShort 310,000 times and DramaWave 290,000 times. The five Chinese-owned short-drama apps drew nearly 2.16 million new installs in October.
 The spread of short dramas is also visible on established video platforms such as YouTube. According to YouTube, views of short dramas on its platform exceeded 6.5 billion in the first half of this year alone, up 50% from the first half of last year. South Korea is growing even faster: from July last year to July this year, views of short-drama videos on YouTube in South Korea surged more than 130%, and watch time rose more than 100% over the same period. "As more short-drama series deliver fast-paced, immersive storytelling, serialized content is rapidly evolving around the vertical screen," YouTube said.
 The market has no clear No. 1 yet, with multiple platforms vying for the lead. The edge for Chinese-owned platforms such as DramaBox and ReelShort is their overwhelming volume of titles and the speed at which they supply new releases. Some productions feature real actors, but a high share of content is made with AI, enabling low-cost mass production. According to China's Xinhua News Agency, the production cost of a high-quality AI-made short drama is about one-tenth that of a live-action one, and production is fast enough to complete 100 episodes in three days. Chinese-owned platforms use AI to quickly churn out provocative material and keep reproducing whatever themes viewers respond to, a strategy aimed at preventing churn.
 Some critics point out that Chinese-owned apps distributing high-intensity content fall into a blind spot in youth protection. Lee Jung-hun, a lawmaker from South Korea's Democratic Party, noted during the National Assembly's Science, ICT, Broadcasting and Communications Committee audit in October that DramaBox and DramaWave, which have operators based in Singapore, are excluded from the requirement to designate a youth protection officer. "Provocative short-drama content and advertising are spreading, but the number of related reviews is zero," Lee said, calling for regulatory improvements.
 The trend is expected to weigh on South Korea's content industry. South Korean operators with their own production capabilities and platforms are losing ground in the battle for users, while Chinese-owned platforms that hold an edge in production cost and supply speed dominate the market, according to industry assessments. As short dramas establish themselves as a revenue model combining advertising and paid subscriptions, industry observers say the need is growing both for South Korean platforms' response strategies and for regulatory fixes, including youth protection.
